title: Druxt Auth 0.5.0; two ways to sign in without leaving your site
description: Simple OAuth 6 removed the password grant. Druxt Auth 0.5.0 gets it working again through a contrib module, and the authorization code grant now takes credentials too, so a Nuxt frontend signs people in without sending them to Drupal.

content.html: Every Druxt site I have built signs people in by sending them somewhere else to do it: out to Drupal's login page, on to a consent screen, and eventually back. With Druxt Auth 0.5.0 the username and password can now be handled entirely in the frontend instead, either through the authorization code grant or through the password grant.
If you have not used it, Druxt Auth wires Nuxt's auth module to Simple OAuth on the Drupal side. It targets Nuxt 2 today, because @nuxtjs/auth-next does.

content.alt: The druxtjs.org playground rendering an Umami recipe block, with a Sign in to edit dialog open over it
content.caption: Signing in happens on the page you were already on.

content.html: The first is the authorization code grant, which now takes credentials directly. Druxt Auth signs the visitor in through Drupal's JSON login route first, so the authorize step finds a session waiting and returns a code without rendering anything:

content.title: Authorization code, handed credentials
content.highlighted: // Nuxt 2 await $auth.loginWith('drupal-authorization_code', { credentials: { name, pass }, })

content.html:
• No client secret in the app: underneath it is still authorization code with PKCE.
  • You get a real Drupal session, which matters if your editors work in Drupal's admin pages through the frontend, and logout() ends it.
  • Drupal and the frontend have to look like one site to the browser, so it needs the proxy.

The second is the password grant. I shipped it in 0.4.0, then Simple OAuth 6 took the grant out of Drupal and took mine with it. 0.5.0 gets it working again, against Simple OAuth Password Grant, the contrib module that puts it back:

content.title: Password grant, through the server route
content.highlighted: // Nuxt 2 await $auth.loginWith('drupal-password', { data: { username, password }, })

content.html:
• No redirect, and no proxy needed: the credentials go to Drupal's token endpoint through Druxt Auth's own server route.
  • That route needs a server, so a statically generated site is out.
  • Tokens and nothing else. Drupal's own pages stay anonymous however signed in the frontend looks, until you set passwordSession, which does need the proxy.
Neither needs a form from you. 0.5.0 ships the sign-in too, a DruxtAuthLogin component and a Nuxt page at /user/login. Drop your own component of that name into components/ and it takes over.

Both post credentials to an endpoint rather than to Drupal's login form, and that form is where Drupal hangs the rest of logging in. TFA interposes there. So does a forced password change, a terms-of-service gate, and anything else that alters it. Skip the form and you skip all of that, and so does anyone else who has the password.

content.alt: Drupal's authorization dialog: You are allowing druxtjs.org to, three role scopes listed, with Allow and Deny buttons
content.caption: Drupal asking the visitor to allow the frontend. The redirect shows this, and the login form before it. Neither grant shows either screen.

content.html: Rate limiting survives, in two places rather than one. The credential sign-in goes through core's auth controller, so core's flood control runs. The password grant never reaches that controller, so the contrib module runs its own flood control, registering under oauth2_password_grant.failed_login_ip rather than user.failed_login_ip. If someone is locked out that way, clearing the core flood entries will not release them.

None of that makes either grant wrong, but it does make them a trade: the trip to Drupal was what ran those checks. Where you still need them, the redirect has not gone anywhere, and calling loginWith without credentials asks for it. The case people ask about is two factor, and it does work that way. I have it running on another site I maintain. It is not pretty: two factor means the full round trip. I want to fix that.

paragraphs.title: What the login form was doing for you

content.html: Origin matters for the authorization code option, and only that one. The session cookie from its JSON login has to reach the authorize request, so druxt: { proxy: { api: true } } is what makes it work at all. Without it the form falls back to the redirect. Across separate domains the cookie would be third party, so there the redirect is your only way in. The password grant has no such constraint.

Consumers are next. A Consumer cannot be public and confidential at once, so a site running both flows needs two, with passwordClientId for the second. It also has to authorize automatically, or the visitor sees Drupal's consent page anyway. On Simple OAuth 6 you need an OAuth2 scope too, because it refuses every authorization request until one exists.

The last is behaviour, not configuration. A Drupal session already open in the browser is refused, rather than signing the visitor in as whoever left it there. The error sets sessionInUse so your form can say why. To end that session instead, point sessionLogout at a route you write yourself in Drupal. Core will not do it.

paragraphs.title: What you have to get right

content.html: I rebuilt druxtjs.org this month so Druxt renders its own docs, every docs page a node and the navigation a menu. It is one of several sites I run Druxt on myself, and what breaks there gets fixed before 2.0.0.

content.alt: A phone screen showing the sign-in dialog, credentials entered, then the tutorial page with an avatar in the header and an editor bar along the bottom
content.caption: The password grant on a phone, start to finish, with no navigation in between. The bar along the bottom is the in-page editing this is for.

content.html: The password grant was never Druxt Auth's to give. Simple OAuth 6 removed it because the OAuth security best practice says it must not be used, and only Drupal's OAuth server can mint a token.

Simple OAuth Password Grant puts it back, maintained by Christoph Niedermoser and Christian Foidl. Their README is blunt about it: use it with great care, for trusted first-party applications, and prefer the authorization code grant where you can. Thank you both for your contribution.

So which one fits? If you can run a server and tokens are all you need, the password grant. If your editors work in Drupal's admin pages through the frontend, or you want to keep the door open for two factor, the authorization code grant. How are you signing people in today? I would like to know.
If either is useful to you, 0.5.0 is out now:

content.title: Install
content.highlighted: composer require 'drupal/simple_oauth_password_grant' npm install druxt-auth@^0.5

paragraphs.title: Who put the password grant back

content.description: Druxt Auth, and the example app that runs both flows against a real Drupal. Sponsorship is what keeps Druxt maintained.
